topic: Why static shocks are worse in winter

script.voiceText: [deep, cinematic documentary narrator, calm authority, crisp pace] You reach for the doorknob... SNAP. [playful, curious, quick] Ouch! Why is it worse in winter? As you walk, charge moves between your shoes and the carpet. In humid air, a film of moisture lets that charge leak away. But winter air is dry, and heating dries it more. So the charge builds, up to tens of thousands of volts. Tens of THOUSANDS? Isn't that deadly? No. The current is tiny, and it's over in millionths of a second. That's why a humidifier helps: wetter air drains the charge. That spark is a tiny lightning bolt... and YOU made it.

claims.claim: Contact and separation of materials (shoes, carpet) transfers charge (triboelectric charging); moisture in the air normally lets charge dissipate, so dry winter air (worsened by indoor heating) lets it build.
claims.source: McGill Office for Science and Society, on static electricity in winter

claims.claim: Walking across carpet can generate about 35,000 V at 10-20% relative humidity versus about 1,500 V at 65-90%.
claims.source: Typical measured static charges table (US Navy electricity/electronics training series, reproduced by tpub)

claims.claim: The discharge carries a very small current and lasts microseconds.
claims.source: ESD human-body-model references (rfwireless-world ESD basics; tpub table notes)
